Mr. Speaker, this government's decision to axe The Canadian is a direct attack on the regions of Canada. Ridings such as mine, Kenora-Rainy River, feel that they have been abandoned by this government.
The withdrawal of The Canadian does not make any sense. In fact, VIA Rail's own documents show that The Canadian was the fourth busiest in Canada, carrying more than half a million people a year with the best occupancy rate on the system, 70 per cent annually and 94 per cent in the peak summer season. If this government had put money into new and upgraded equipment, it would have been able to save many of the routes it has cut. Instead, it chose to attack once more the regions of Canada. The constituents of Kenora-Rainy River and many millions of Canadians will not forget this travesty of justice.

Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, the National Council of Welfare released its study of the effects of this government's plans to claw back family allowance and old age pensions. It states that in spite of the Prime Minister's protestations to the contrary, the clawback proposal signals an end to the longstanding Canadian principle of universality. A social program that delivers benefits to everyone and then collects them all back from some recipients is not universal.

According to the study by the National Council of Welfare, the government is undermining family allowances and old age pensions. These new measures, which are discriminatory and increasingly complex, are gradually threatening the universality of our social programs. By eliminating universality of family allowances, reducing unemployment benefits and backtracking on child care promises this government is dismantling, in five years, a social policy framework that it took Canada a century to construct. Canadians are saying that it is enough.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read about and heard from a number of people who are suggesting that we lower the rate, but let me comment for a minute on the Conference Board proposal.
It has come up with a proposal for a 7 per cent rate but in that proposal it has exaggerated the price effect, the difference between a 7 per cent and a 9 per cent rate rate. In addition to that, it has left a $3 billion gap in the reduction of the rate from 9 per cent to 7 per cent.

Now in response to the hon. member's question, I have said all along that this is a GST system, a package. It includes a GST credit or a rebate to low income Canadians. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. Last week in announcing a toxic waste clean-up program the minister indicated that Canadian toxic wastes would be incinerated in Canada. He said: "We will not destroy them in England. We will not destroy them on the planet Mars. We will have to destroy them here in Canada".
Despite this commitment the minister's department had just days earlier given permission to allow the shipment of contaminated wastes from Quebec to France for destruction.
Will the minister explain this inconsistency between his words and the actions of his department? Will he explain why he said earlier today that he does not have the power to prevent this shipment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the member to give the full quote on the expression of the government's policy on PCB exportation. What I said on behalf of the government was that there would be no more exports of federal PCBs to foreign countries for destruction and that we would try to reduce to the minimum the export of private PCBs to foreign countries for destruction.
Those PCBs which left Montreal last night are not federal PCBs; they are private PCBs.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
They left for France and the reason we have not stopped the shipment is that we had no legal reason to do so. I had extensive consultations with the government's legal experts, and I was advised that we have no legal grounds to act because the shipment complies completely with federal government requirements.
October 25, 1989

I will not expose this government to the embarrassment of having a decision quashed by the courts as was done in Quebec the other day. I have instructed the officials in my department to examine the possibilities of enacting new regulations to control completely the export of PCBs.
Mr. Speaker, I find it strange that in an area of national interest there would be a difference between local PCBs and government PCBs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are privatizing PCBs.

Sections 41 to 45 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act give the minister the power to make regulations prohibiting the import or export of toxic wastes. Under Section 35 of that act the minister can issue an interim order in the absence of adequate regulations.
Will the minister undertake to issue such an order immediately?

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course there is a distinction to draw between the two regulations that have been quoted. The last one is in case of immediate danger. I was advised by the officials last night that there was no danger to invoke in this case.
The other regulation is a general one, and we are in the process of examining the possibility of enacting such a regulation in the next week. We will keep Parliament posted.

I wish to say a few words in presenting this report, Mr. Speaker. The public accounts committee today tables a report which addresses significant concerns in the areas of government food inspection, pesticide regulation and controls against the spread of plant and animal diseases.
Canadians continue to have confidence in the safety of the food supply. In order to maintain this confidence, as the audit considered by the committee pointed out, there is a need to assess risks to human health and allocate resources to the areas of highest risk.
While the Department of Agriculture which is responsible for the food production and inspection branch has responded positively to the audit, the committee is calling upon the Auditor General to assess the department's progress in this follow-up audit. In particular, the committee was not satisfied with the low quality of information presented to Parliament in the department's annual spending estimates, Part III of the estimates documents, and has recommended improvements in this regard.
The committee also recommends amendments to the import control provisions of legislation and regulations to help improve procedures that guard against the spread of animal and plant diseases. Finally, concerns were expressed about improved training of food inspectors and better management of labour relations in the department.

This government from time to time has gone on at great length to say that we have to return the unemployment insurance system to the principles of insurability and that it should have some relevance to the purposes for which the unemployment insurance system was first designed.
But this bill not only introduces one of the most unfair kinds of taxation systems imaginable but, in terms of social cost accounting, it is moving 180 degrees in the opposite direction from which anyone with any modicum of common sense at all ought to be considering. We are asking working people and their employers, regardless of their ability to pay, be they workers or employers, to pay more for longer periods to get less for shorter periods. Obviously that does not make sense. It certainly is not justice and it certainly is not fair.
I have worked with many working people in the some 21 years I spent in the hourly paid labour force in several industries. Those who have worked for 10 or 20 years and are fortunate enough never to find themselves unemployed for a long enough period of time to collect at least know that some of the people they work with are going to benefit from the UI program. They say: "Well, even though I never got anything out of it and I have been paying all these years, at least my workmates get something".
Now we are asking them to pay for education programs and to go even further along the path which was set under the Liberal administration a few years ago. They are paying more for what should be economic development programs and job creation programs. Those programs may be fine. They may be dandy, and maybe we are not going to argue with those particular programs at all, although some of them have had pretty patchy records from time to time. On what basis of common sense or any other kind of reasoning do we suggest that these programs have any relationship at all to an individual employee's or employer's record of employment or unemployment? There is just no basis in reasoning.
Some of the other measures that are being taken within Bill C-21 have been required by court action to extend maternity benefits into paternal benefits are good. While we have not taken issue with them within the context of Bill C-21, I am one of those who have wondered for some time just what the hell they have got to do with employment and unemployment in terms of unemployment insurance premiums.
Where is the relationship between whether somebody is employable or unemployable depending upon the vagaries of their particular company or industry? These are good programs but they have no connection to an unemployment insurance program. It is fraudulent to suggest that they do. We are compounding that fraud by all of these changes, both in internal financing and the kinds of programs we are asking the UIC fund to pay, that is the whole thrust of Bill C-21.
When a measure is so far out and so incomprehensible in terms of the aims and objectives of unemployment insurance as is this, it is hard to know how to force yourself to deal with some of the detailed matters arising out of the legislation. When the entire concept is screwy, it is hard to do what you think is just wasting your time talking about the dotted i's and the crossed t's.
Other changes have been made from time to time in answer to the kinds of reactions arising from some sections of the labour force and some sections of the business community, that say we have to tighten up the rules, tighten up the periods and qualifications, et cetera. We bring in new regulations. Some ordinary employees work 5, 10, 15 or 20 years and never collect UI often never collecting during their entire lives. If they do find themselves suddenly thrown out of work, having been laid off and honestly unemployed after having paid the premiums, they go to the UI office and they make a claim. While some of the trick questions and various other methods that have been brought into the system over the years to stop abuses of the system do not do a very good job of stopping or dissuading those few who want to cheat this system and any system, these methods do an excellent job of discouraging and cheating these honest employees who, once every 10 or 20 years, find themselves on the unemployment lines. They are the ones who get shafted.
October 25, 1989

Surely we have been at this business of unemployment insurance long enough that anyone who has been a member of Parliament for a few months, not to mention several years as a number of the members opposite have been, should know that those workers are the people who get hurt every time we tighten the screws, and not the ones who Parliament has supposedly been after. So why do we keep doing it? Is it our intent to shaft honest employers and honest employees? I cannot believe that, but after experiencing this place off and on for a number of years I am really left wondering just what kind of motivations we have when we continue to abuse this entire system and the people who should be the honest beneficiaries of it in times of their own peril.
Most working people are honest, most are hard working, most employees and most employers do not mind paying their share. But in terms of equity, why should an employer who is operating a very marginal business in terms of profit, or may in fact be suffering a loss, have to pay exactly the same amount of taxes per employee as a corporation which may have been in the enviable position of earning hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars in profit over the preceding year? What kind of sense of equity brings about a system in which we not only place 100 per cent of the responsibility for payment on those employers and their employees but in which we add a whole host of other programs; social programs, maternity benefits, paternal benefits, job training strategies, education programs and everything else that should properly come out of general revenue based upon ability to pay, and put them onto the backs of those employers and those employees?
The entire system, as we are amending it, is making less and less and less sense every year. If our constituents from one end of the country to the other, from cities and rural areas and the resource hinterlands of this country are up in arms, if they are feeling that nobody really gives a damn about them and nobody in Parliament really gives a damn about any sense of equity or justice, then we can hardly blame them. If we and this institution become held in contempt for what we are doing to those people,
Government Orders
I, for one, think that they are entirely justified if we go by the track record of this Parliament in recent years.

Mr. Speaker, the bill that we are considering would seek to drastically change the unemployment insurance regime, a system that has served this country veiy well. In so many other institutions or programs, be it medicare, pensions or any other item that I could mention to you in the arena of government activities there are abuses. Thke medicare, for example. It is not difficult for us to demonstrate that in the medicare area there are abuses. But who is there among us who would suggest that we ought to throw out medicare, that we ought to disrupt the basic system, that we ought to throw out the baby with the bath water? Surely there is a better way.
I submit to you that if these changes go through, if this savage piece of legislation goes through, if the government has its way in gutting the unemployment insurance system, it will have thrown out the baby with the bath water, it will have destroyed a system, a program that has served this country very well.
I hear some among us in this Chamber talk about the lazy people. I have heard it again and again, muttered at first, but now they are getting a little braver because they are beginning to realize that a number of their colleagues over there share the view that somehow people who draw unemployment insurance are lazy.
They ought to have been with me today when I was travelling back from my constituency of Burin-St. George's. At the airport in Stephenville I talked to a lady from one of the nearby communities, a married woman who has three children aged 9, 11 and 13. She was doing what tens of thousands of Newfoundlanders have done over the years. She had the option of staying put and drawing unemployment insurance at the present rate, not at the doctored rate, the diminished rate that we will have if and when this bill goes through. She had that option, but instead last night she packed her suitcase and left her children in the charge of a family member. As I speak she is in Toronto looking for a job. I said to her; "Did you have a job or some indication of a job before you decided to go?" She said: "No, I have to go. I have no choice."

October 25, 1989
Government Orders
She has a choice of sorts. She can stay home and draw that unemployment insurance and be with her loved ones including her three children, or she can go and seek employment. She is doing what the thousands of Newfoundlanders who live in Fort McMurray, Cambridge, Toronto, Halifax and Vancouver do; what the hundreds from my riding who work on the CP tracks from Saskatchewan through to B.C. every summer for many months do; and what the hundreds more who work on the Great Lakes boats for eight or nine months a year away from their families do.
I have to tell you that as a Newfoundlander I am insulted, absolutely insulted, by the pious suggestions of those people who tell us they will save us from ourselves, who tell us they will help us stop being lazy. I have news for you. It is not laziness that has put many of my fellow Newfoundlanders on the receiving end of unemployment insurance over the years, not laziness but absolute, dire necessity.
As in the example I just gave you of the mother with the three children, even when they have the option of receiving unemployment insurance benefits many of them opt to go and look for something better.
Other of my colleagues here on this side of the House will be making points about the individual problems with this legislation. I just want in passing to mention a couple, but I then want to get back on a theme that I think might help members of this House understand why it is the unemployment insurance system ought not to be savaged in the way it will be with this legislation.
The longer qualification period and the shorter benefit period are two proposed provisions which will play a lot of havoc in the area I represent. Why is that? Is it a game because they do not want to go to work? No, it is because there is no work to go to.
It is all very well for somebody who lives in southern Ontario where the economy is moving along quite fine, thank you very much, to sit in judgment on those who receive unemployment insurance benefits. It is a very different matter for those on the receiving end, a very different manner indeed.
You have to look at Newfoundland and other parts of rural Canada in this particular context. In so far as Newfoundland is concerned, and my riding of Burin-St. George's, many of the jobs are by nature seasonal occupations. That is not to anybody's blame; it is just the way it is. It is difficult in parts of Newfoundland to catch
fish through three feet of ice. It is difficult to catch fish when the Arctic ice is moving down from Greenland as it does on the northeast coast of Newfoundland, sometimes as late as June. It is foolhardy to be putting nets out there if they are going to be mowed down by an iceberg several times as high as your house.
There are realities out there. If you extract a livelihood from the harsh resources of the North Atlantic there are some realities. One of them is: just as you do not stand in front of a truck in downtown Toronto unless you have a short-term objective, you do not put your boat or nets in front of an iceberg.
All those people who piously tell us about how they are going to save Canada from lazy people ought to take a trip to Newfoundland or take a trip to Cambridge, Ontario, or Fort McMurray and have a look at the lazy Newfoundlanders they are muttering about.
They will find a couple of things if they have done a survey. They will find there are more native bom Newfoundlanders living outside Newfoundland today than there are in Newfoundland. I wonder why. It is because they had enough get up and go to get up and go to where the jobs are. But some of them, for many reasons, have not had that option open to them.
We are fed up with being characterized as a bunch of lazies because we happen to take advantage of a program that was designed for our kind in the beginning.
What is our kind? It is the kind of people who through no fault of their own have to find a way to bridge themselves between seasonal job opportunities. That is what the guts of this program is all about. That is why I get upset that the government is wanting to take the guts out of this program and that is what it is doing with this legislation, make no mistake about it.
It is Tory resettlement 1989 style. It is a cowardly, not too well disguised attempt to encourage people to move to urban Canada. Well, we have news for them. I see from your signal, Sir, that my time has run out. If I had more time I would tell you what that news is.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, for now I give you notice that if this government, through unemployment insurance wrecking, through the closing of post offices, through the shutting down and abandoning of railway lines, through the foisting upon people of another tax which they cannot pay, insists on trying to shut down rural Canada as it is doing, the public will have a message for it come the next election.
October 25, 1989

Maybe what ought to be done, I say to my good friend for Burlington whose heart is in the right place but whose head is all tangled up with the wrong gang, is to go back and, instead of bringing in those semantic rules, those changes which mean nothing, do the people of Canada who have helped build this country from coast to coast a favour, do them a service instead of being party to the insult that somehow they are lazy because they need assistance from the public purse once in a while, until the seasonal job comes around again, until they can of their own resources provide the livelihood for their family and their loved ones.

Mr. Speaker, it is with no great pleasure again that I stand here to debate Bill C-21. After having gone through the closure motions which we went through yesterday and the Draconian actions which this government has put this Parliament through in order that it would hear as little debate as possible on this measure, there is no joy in getting up to speak to it.
When we look at such measures in Bill C-21 as major and minor attachment to the workforce, the natural question to ask is: What does that mean? What it means in its essence is that those who are least advantaged in our society are going to be the ones who suffer the most.
Who are the least advantaged in our society, or the most disadvantaged, whichever way you would like to put it, Mr. Speaker? We find there are several groups of people within that description, but certainly there are those who are less well educated and there are those who work part time, and both groups contain a preponderance of women. In the final analysis, those who are going to be most severely affected by these changes to Bill C-21, and most other changes as well, are women.
For the government to come in with such a change to the act is an indication which I think can be traced to free trade. It can be traced to these fine schemes the government has for forcing the Canadian workforce to be competitive.
Government Orders
Those are phrases which we often hear the government refer to in defence of any number of things it is proposing, all the way from the general sales tax. These references are couched in language that it is trying to do something with the deficit and the national debt and so on. Of course, there have been references as well to Bill C-21 in the same context, trying to become competitive, and free trade is involved in it as well. Of course, competitiveness was one of the reasons that the government kept referring to as the necessity for getting free trade.
When we talk about competitiveness the implication is always that Canadian workers are really overpaid. When the government talks about competitiveness, it talks about lean and mean. When the government talks about reductions, it talks about social programs. There are any number of our competitors who have better social programs than Canada does.
It makes you wonder, but not for long, what the government is talking about when it talks about "competitive". The reason you do not have to wonder very long, Mr. Speaker, is that you suddenly realize that what they are talking about is our competitiveness in relation not to the more progressive countries of this world but to the least progressive countries of this world.
Members of the committee on the government side have even made direct references to how well off Canada is in relation to, I am not sure whether it was Bangladesh or the Philippines or some other very seriously disadvantaged country.
Why is the government putting in these measures in Bill C-21? When we look at the government's own impact study, we find an admission which I would be ashamed to do if I were the government. It admits that right off the top there are going to be 30,000 Canadians eliminated altogether from being able to benefit from unemployment insurance.
There have been more credible studies, I would suggest, which have shown that in the neighbourhood of
130,000	Canadians will be excluded entirely from unemployment insurance benefits, not 30,000. One hundred thousand more Canadians will be excluded entirely from unemployment insurance after the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act goes in compared to those who are able to access it now.

October 25, 1989
Government Orders
We are going to create a very large class of very poor people, again, as I said, mostly poorly educated and mostly women. It is not a marvel when you look at those countries which so often are implicated in the government's statements that we need to become more competitive, that in those countries in what are commonly called unfortunately the Third World countries, we find that the people who are abused by the multinational corporations and their own governments are the poor and that they are mostly women.
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, consciously or unconsciously one of the main consequences of these changes to C-21 which the government is bringing in will be that in Canada, in preparation for an even broader free trade agreement with what we often hear the government refer to as the Pacific Rim, we will be setting up people who will be glad, because they are not able to even get the poorly paid minimum wage jobs that are available in this country now.
The minimum wage is something else we could talk about. I would remind the countiy that the federal government's minimum wage is the lowest in the country. At best on the government's minimum wage a single person anywhere in the countiy would make half as much as the poverty line in this countiy.
This bill is setting up Canadians for the multinationals to come in and use those poor people, to use those women in exactly the same way as they are being used in the Third World countries; for the menial, repetitious tasks which experience has shown time and time again wear these people out in three to five years. In many instances they are not able to continue to any other kind of employment, because of perhaps poor eyesight or because of the totally debilitating postures they have developed due to the conditions under which they have been forced to work, than going on the streets as prostitutes.
I would suggest that this bill is moving Canada very, very close to that line. With the spread to the Pacific Rim trading, to the Pacific Rim free trade deal, I predict that this is precisely one of the effects that this bill is going to have.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for allowing me the opportunity to address Bill C-21 on changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I see that the hon. member opposite is grinning with the same kind of grin that the government is giving all of us who are very concerned about the changes in this bill; a kind of grin that says "the heck with you" because we are putting forth some changes and even though we are following a procedure that, as my colleague to the left has said, is Draconian in the extreme, we are going to put it through. Even if the contents of this bill go counter to all the principles that Canadians have come to regard as being part and parcel of this nation's fabric, principles that have taken us 100 years to build up as part of the Canadian character, we are going to shove it through without the appropriate debate.
I am pleased that we have at least a modicum of opportunity to address some of the amendments that are here before us, amendments that have been made necessary, quite frankly, because the bill does not do what it ought to do, namely, to address the unemployment problem in this country, most of it structurally.
I have heard the government members over the course of several days spread out over several months-because we have had such limited time to debate this bill in this House-read out some statistics about the greatness of their job programs. Nothing could be further from the truth. In fact, the unemployment rates for the post-recession period, for the post-growth period that is supposedly unprecedented in the history of this country, are much higher than they were in the pre-recession period. In fact, what is very, very telling is that the structural unemployment rate in 1988, according to StatsCanada, is much higher.
I know the parliamentary secretary is trying to represen rate in 1988, according to StatsCanada, is much higher, watching him carefully on the monitor to make sure that things are being waded through properly. But I draw to his attention that the structural unemployment rate in 1988, five years after we began a post-recession period of unprecedented growth, sits at 8.3 per cent. That is 5 per cent higher than it was before this countiy entered into a recession.
October 25, 1989

That structural unemployment rate is verified in the doubling of a rate amongst older workers. In 1982, for example, as Canada was going into a recession, the structural unemployment rate among seniors was at 7.7 per cent and today it sits at 14.8 per cent. The prime structural rate nationally sits at 7.7 whereas prior to the recession and prior to all this growth it was at 5.6 per cent. The duration of unemployment in 1982, the duration of time that people spent on unemployment benefits if they found themselves without employment in 1982, prior to this country entering a recession, was 15.7 weeks for the average claimant. For the average claimant at the end of 1988, according to StatsCan figures, in a period of unprecedented growth, the duration was 19.1 weeks per claimant.
These figures beg the question why, why Bill C-21? What is this bill doing to address the structural unemployment of this country? What is this bill doing to address the longer term of unemployment in this country? What is this bill doing to address the varying disparities nationally among our regions?
Precious little, Mr. Speaker. I give you an example. The government has spent much time, through its members, reading statistics about how it is going to put in more moneys. Instead of putting moneys into income maintenance for claimants it is going to put moneys into job creation programs, into job entry, into job development, into skill shortages, into skills investment and community futures. Well, I think it is important and instructive for us all, for the nation, to understand what the government is doing. It is important so that the nation-all peoples watching this debate which has been shortened by the government's desire to pass through a bill very quickly without having the nation wake up to discover what is happening to it and to its citizens-can judge.
Let me read some of the figures because they are in juxtaposition with the minister's words. It is appropriate for all of us to wonder which speak the truth; the words of the minister and her government or the statistics of the moneys that the government is actually putting forward in these job training programs in job development.
For 1989, according to the Estimates, there was a net decrease of 8 per cent of funds available for job develop-
Govemment Orders
ment. For job entry there was a net decrease of 1.7 over 1988. The skill shortages area is extremely important because the minister is justifying the changes to the unemployment insurance bill on the basis that we require greater skills amongst our labour force. What she has done is decreased-that is spelled d-e-c-r-e-a-s-e-d, Mr. Parliamentary Secretary-moneys to the tune of 3.6 per cent. She has dropped the amount of money in skills investment by 7 per cent. She has dropped the amount of moneys for Community Futures by 2.5 per cent. She has dropped the amount of moneys available for Innovations by 20 per cent over the last year.
Mr. Speaker and hon. members, I ask you, is this an indication of a government that is telling the truth, or is this an indication of a government whose actions speak a greater lie than its words?
One need only take a look at some of the clauses that this government would ram through. For example, it is unprepared to support a motion by my hon. colleague for Notre-Dame-de-Grace in the area of benefits for people who adopt children. We have seen a reduction of unemployment benefits for such purposes go from 15 to 10 weeks, where the amendment of my colleague says, "Let us substitute the word "ten" for "fifteen". What happens? The government says, "No, no, no, we cannot support that. We are going to make some mealy-mouthed approach to the fact that we are going to rectify a problem". The government introduces a clause that is going to implement a means test from which only those who have the patience of Job will be able to profit.
That would be bad enough, but we take this very miserly and vicious attitude towards helping to develop a labour force for refer to as an equally vicious subclause in clause 19 of this bill. In addition to giving the government the power to change the unemployment insurance fund from an income maintenance program to a training type of program, it privatizes unemployment insurance and gives the government the authority to take a grand total of about 15 per cent of all funds from premiums and apply them to training programs, training programs which obviously it is not at all favouring, if we accept the Statistics Canada figures that I just read a few moments ago, figures that are corroborated by the department.

October 25, 1989
Government Orders
The estimates for Canadian Jobs Strategy, the amount of moneys that are going to be generated by this adjustment in the training program run at about $1.4 billion and the unemployment insurance bill is going to be greater than that. What will happen is that the government, with a sleight of hand, will move moneys out of unemployment insurance premiums into Canadian Jobs Strategy. Well, thank you very much. Let us suppose that this is going to serve the people of Canada, it is going to serve the labour of this country. What about those claimants to unemployment insurance who face an employment counsellor and say, "I do not want to accept unemployment insurance. I want to go on a training program".
I draw your attention to Clause 19, Mr. Speaker. Claimants cannot appeal the decision of an employment counsellor. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, as I ask all members on the opposite side of the House and on this side of the House; if we are truly interested in developing a skilled labour market for all of Canada, should we not at least give them the right of appeal? I guess the answer is that the working people of Canada are going to be treated with the same contemptuous arrogance with which this House has been dealt by the minister and this government in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House focuses on the provisions of this legislation which discriminate against new claimants for unemployment and, in particular, young people. The bill discriminates, therefore, against those who have the greatest difficulty in surviving economically and socially. Once again we have an example of the government's actions confounding the government's rhetoric. Once again, the government contributes to the unnecessary divide that is building in this country between the affluent and the less well-to-do. Once again, the government pushes away from the family table the least advantaged, in this case Canada's unemployed young people.
I want to address one set of consequences of this legislation that has not so far received much focus. I speak in part in my capacity as critic for the Solicitor General's Department for our party.
It is fitting that we raise the issue of the impact on crime prevention in this country of this legislation because today the Solicitor General with a lot of PR fanfare announced Crime Prevention Week. The hypocrisy of this government knows no bounds. The very week it asked Canada in sanctimonious terms to participate in crime prevention it guts one of the key programs that
gives some hope of preventing increased crime in Canada.
Two weeks ago in Montreal an international conference of experts and civic leaders was sponsored by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. This conference included guests and delegates from Europe and throughout North America. Included in the sponsors was the European Forum on Urban Security and the U.S. Conference on Mayors in collaboration with the Montreal Urban Community, five international organizations of cities and more than 30 partners. They received over 100 briefs. They had delegates from 31 countries around the world and were addressed by the Under Secretary General of the United Nations, the Secretary General of the Council of Europe, ministers from France, the Netherlands and Canada, as well as mayors from Canada's and the world's major cities.
At this conference the federal government gave merely passing attention. Two of the ministers dropped in to give speeches and disappeared. The speeches, if I may say, were marked by bromidic cliches. In the follow-up seminar after the conference the Minister of Justice did not even appear himself. He sent his Parliamentary Secretary who did not take the trouble to even understand what the seminar was about.
The overwhelming conclusion of this major international conference was that community must be the focal point of crime prevention, and that we must go beyond the criminal justice system in seeking a solution to the rising crime rate in Canada and throughout the world. Crime prevention must focus on social development, it was said in this important conference. The causes of crime, as we have known for years include poverty, unemployment, lack of affordable, decent housing and an unresponsive education system. It is particularly among our young people that unemployment has the effect of moving them to crime, and crime is largely centred among our young people.
We were treated in the seminar after the conference to a very important paper based on a study in the U.K. by a David Farrington and a Donald J. West. This study surveyed over the last 25 years 400 young people in London and traced their development from about age eight or nine to now when they are into their mid-thirties. They were able to interview in their most recent round somewhere over 90 per cent of the participants back in the early 1960s. They were able to look at those who got into trouble with the law and who had contributed to the rising crime rate in Britain. They were able to make some analysis of what it was that distinguished those who got into trouble from those who did not.
October 25, 1989

The overwhelming conclusion was the conclusion which the conference itself reached. In order to prevent the development of crime and antisocial behaviour, social prevention programs are vitally needed. These could begin, and I quote: "by targeting three important predictors of offending that may be both causal and modifiable"-sociological words at their best-"economic deprivation, school failure and poor parental child rearing behaviour". What this points to is a combination of programs, but a combination in which dealing with youth unemployment is absolutely essential.
Britain, under the Prime Minister's friend Margaret Thatcher, tried to do what this government is doing in a slightly different way. They cut off young people from unemployment insurance, or the British version thereof, between the ages of 16 and 18. That change lasted for barely a year. Margaret Thatcher herself finally understood the impact of that on the other issue which she was concerned with, which was crime in British cities. She changed her position entirely. The government was forced to reverse that decision and to reinstitute unemployment insurance for the 16 to 18 year olds in Britain.
If this government is serious about crime prevention, if it wants to do more than rhetoric, it must withdraw this bill and completely revamp the provisions applicable to young people in Canada.
UI is a major federal program. It is one of the points at which the federal government directly intervenes in the social systems in Canada. It gives the federal government some very real leverage in trying to cope with the social problems that are hitting our cities and our countryside. The delicate fabric of our social system is critical to the fight against illegal drugs and crime that accompanies that dreadful traffic.
I plead with the government to take this issue more seriously than it has. What we have seen all summer is a situation in which the government has simply pretended to listen. It has reduced the number of hearings that it has held and wants to hold across the country. It has said
Government Orders
from the outset that it is not going to accept changes, and we have seen that reaction so far in the House. It has turned a deaf ear to the pleas of the people from every section of this country not to proceed with these changes, not to do this unravelling of a critical social program for the people of this country.
At the conference I referred to earlier some of the speakers revealed the two world visions that now face us when we look at the changing social conditions since the end of the Second World War, the rapid urbanization, the tremendous growth in poverty around the world, the changing economic system that is imposing changes on the social, political and economic systems around the world.
We in the west have two possible responses, two opposite visions that we can put forward. We can put forward the vision of a Ronald Reagan or a Margaret Thatcher or the Prime Minister of this country, which is of two nations, of two worlds-a rich world and a poor world. The rich can increasingly build a bunker around themselves and try to fend off the legitimate cries for equality, the legitimate cries for a place at the table. Or we can move to a different vision, a vision at which we first begin by recognizing that the world is a family, that we are all one, and that our obligation as members of Parliament and as public servants is to tiy not to narrow the access to the riches that this country and this world can produce but instead to broaden the access to those riches and that a country is going to be measured not by the wealth of its richest citizens, but by how we treat our poor and, in particular, our young people who must begin by building a world of hope. Only then can we begin seriously and realistically to deal with the problems that confront us.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Has the time for debate expired? If that is the case, I want to again say in the strongest terms that by using closure in this debate the government has shown complete contempt for democracy as many points have not been made in this debate.

Hear, hear!

October 25, 1989

I will do the grouping on Motions Nos. 15, 16 and 18. Motions Nos. 15, 16 and 18 were grouped for debate. A vote on Motion No. 15 applies to Motions Nos. 16 and 18.

Motion No. 15
That Bill C-21 be amended in Clause 11 by adding immediately after line 7 at page 10 the following:

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any responsibility more onerous on members than the casting of a vote in division. I have some doubts about the wisdom of standing up 24 times, but when the results of the last vote were announced, there was a total of 38 members present in the chamber on the opposition side and I suspect that there were fewer members on our side than the vote count would indicate.
If we fall into sloppy habits in relation to votes, we could get the House and the integrity of Parliament into trouble down the road. I would suggest that members should be present in the chamber to hear the motion read and they should remain in the chamber until the vote is announced or they should not vote.
I would hope that on all sides of the House we might respect that set of principles so that we can have clarity on the results of the votes.

Hear, hear!
